task: Spot attribution bias and escalation early in a cross-border dispute and run a mediation that ends in a written joint plan.
condition: Given a dispute case with two parties, a timeline of events and costs, and a mediator brief.
standard: The memo names the bias and escalation stage correctly, the mediation follows a set order, and the joint plan has owners, dates and a cost split that adds up.
who: Leaders who handle disputes between teams, partners or suppliers in different countries.

modules.title: How disputes grow: the stages of escalation
modules.intro: Disputes grow in steps, from a difference of opinion to a fight over survival. The earlier you place the stage, the cheaper the fix.
points: Stage 2: positions harden and sides form
modules.example: A supplier and a buyer dispute a late delivery. Week 1: emails about the date (stage 1). Week 3: each copies senior managers and blames the other (stage 2). Week 6: the buyer withholds a 90,000 payment and the supplier stops shipping (stage 3). Cost of fixing at week 1: about 5 hours of talk. At week 6: 90,000 frozen plus lost output of 2 weeks.
modules.activity: Read a case timeline and mark the stage at each date with the sign that shows it.
modules.standard: Every date has the correct stage and one named sign.

modules.title: Attribution bias: why we blame character not context
modules.bloom: Understand and apply: explain and test
modules.intro: When others fail, we blame their character. When we fail, we blame the situation. Both sides do this, so each thinks the other is at fault.
points: We explain our lateness by traffic
Test the cause with a list of context facts
modules.example: Team X is 3 days late. Team Y says 'they are careless'. Context list: Team X got specification changes on day 2 and day 6, lost 2 staff to illness, and works on a public holiday cycle of 4 days. Estimated delay from context = 2 days for the two specification changes + 1 day for the staff illness + 4 days for the holiday cycle = 7 days of lost time, more than the 3 days they were late. The data shows context, not carelessness, explains the delay.
modules.activity: For a case, list the blame statements and replace each with a list of context facts and an estimate of their effect.
modules.standard: At least three blame statements converted, each with a context fact and a time or cost estimate.

modules.title: Cultural meanings of conflict, face and honour
modules.intro: In some places open argument shows honesty; in others it causes loss of face. The same act can mean different things.
points: Private talk may save the relationship
Apology may mean respect, not guilt
modules.example: A manager openly corrects a partner's error in a meeting of 12 people. In a face-sensitive setting, the partner loses standing in front of 12 witnesses. Cost estimate: partner stops sharing early warnings, so 1 problem in 4 now surfaces late, adding about 2 weeks each time. Alternative: a private note the same day, correction agreed in 1 conversation.
modules.activity: Rewrite a public correction as a private one and list what each side gains or loses.
modules.standard: A private version with the same facts and at least two gains and losses per side.

modules.title: Reading early warning signs
modules.intro: Before a dispute blows up, signs appear: slower replies, more people copied, formal language, new demands.
points: Watch for a switch to formal or legal wording
modules.example: Reply times in days: week 1, 1; week 2, 2; week 3, 4; week 4, 7. Reply time rose from 1 day to 7 days. People copied: 2, 2, 5, 9. A rise of 7 copied persons in 3 weeks. Rule: if reply time doubles twice and copies triple, call a meeting. Here replies doubled twice by week 3 and copies reached triple (6 or more) only in week 4, when 9 were copied, so by this rule the call was due in week 4.
modules.activity: Plot reply time and copy count over six weeks from given data and mark the trigger week.
modules.standard: Correct trigger week and the rule is stated with numbers.

modules.title: Mediator role and neutral ground
modules.intro: A mediator helps both sides talk and does not decide. We choose who, where and how, so neither side feels outnumbered.
modules.example: Party A is in a city 8 time zones from party B. Choose a video call at a slot that costs each side equal pain: A at 08:00, B at 16:00. Language: neither party's first language, plain English with a written summary after each hour. 3 sessions of 90 minutes = 4.5 hours, against an estimated 2 weeks of lost trade worth 40,000 if unresolved.
modules.activity: Prepare a mediation plan with place, time, language, rules and a written agenda.
modules.standard: The plan names each choice, shows equal burden on the two sides, and states the cost of no agreement.

modules.title: Running a mediation in a set order
modules.intro: A fixed order keeps a heated meeting on track: opening, each side's story, shared issues, options, agreement.
points: Restate the other's view before answering
List issues, then options, then choose
modules.example: Time plan, 90 minutes: opening 10, party A story 15, party B story 15, restate each other 10, issue list 10, options 20, agreement 10 = 90 minutes. Issues listed: late payment 90,000, delivery plan, price review. Options: pay 60,000 now and 30,000 on delivery; weekly status call. Agreed in 90 minutes.
modules.activity: Run a 90-minute role-play mediation with a time plan and record the issues and options.
modules.standard: The agenda adds to 90 minutes, all steps happen in order, and issues and options are written down.

modules.title: Splitting cost and drafting the joint plan
modules.intro: The plan turns talk into action: who does what by when, and who pays what.
points: Each action has an owner and a date
Cost split is shown in numbers
modules.example: Total dispute cost 150,000: 90,000 frozen payment, 40,000 extra freight, 20,000 lost output. The two sides agree cause shares in the session: supplier 45% = 67,500 and buyer 55% = 82,500. Check: 67,500 + 82,500 = 150,000. Actions: supplier ships by 14 June, buyer pays 60,000 by 20 June, review on 1 July.
modules.activity: Write a one-page joint plan from a case with a cost split, actions, owners and dates.
modules.standard: Cost shares add to the total and every action has an owner and date.

modules.title: Joint governance so the dispute does not return
modules.intro: The last step is a simple rule set for the future: how to raise issues early and who meets when.
points: Name a joint contact on each side
modules.example: Rule: if a delivery is more than 2 days late, the contacts call within 1 day. Escalate to directors only if the call fails. Quarterly review of 4 numbers: late deliveries, payment days, open issues, cost of rework. Last year 9 late deliveries of 120 = 7.5%. Target for next year: 4%, which is 5 of 120.
modules.activity: Write a one-page governance brief with triggers, contacts and four numbers for review, and present it in 5 minutes.
modules.standard: Triggers have numbers, review numbers have a baseline and target, and the brief is delivered within 5 minutes.

quiz.q: Week 1 emails about a date, week 3 managers copied and blame, week 6 payment withheld. Name the three stages.
quiz.a: Week 1 is stage 1 (disagree), week 3 stage 2 (sides form), week 6 stage 3 (threats and damage).

quiz.q: Why is it cheaper to deal with a dispute at stage 1?
quiz.a: Only a few hours of talk are needed, with nothing frozen or lost yet.

quiz.q: Context facts add up to 7 days of delay and the team was 3 days late. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: Context, not carelessness, explains the delay.

quiz.q: What is attribution bias in one sentence?
quiz.a: Blaming other people's character for failures but our own situation for ours.

quiz.q: Why can a public correction before 12 people be costly in a face-sensitive setting?
quiz.a: The partner loses standing and may hide later problems, so issues surface late.

quiz.q: Reply times were 1, 2, 4, 7 days. In which week had replies doubled twice?
Why choose a call slot of 08:00 for A and 16:00 for B?
quiz.a: The pain of the hour is shared equally, which supports fairness.

quiz.q: A 90-minute plan has 10, 15, 15, 10, 10, 20 and a last block. How long is the last block?
A 150,000 cost is split 45% and 55%. What are the amounts?
Nine of 120 deliveries were late. What is the rate and what is the 4% target in deliveries?

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Disputes grow in steps
ladder.slide: A dispute moves from talk to hardened sides to damage. Early action is cheap.
ladder.notes: Say: draw the three steps. Check: place a short story. Mistake: waiting for a formal complaint.

ladder.title: L2 Blame and context
ladder.slide: We explain our failures by context and theirs by character. Test by listing the context facts.
ladder.notes: Say: give a late-train story. Check: learners list facts. Mistake: treating the list as an excuse.

ladder.title: L3 Face and honour
ladder.slide: Public correction can cost trust. A private route often keeps the facts and the relationship.
ladder.notes: Say: compare two versions. Check: same facts in both. Mistake: thinking private means soft.

ladder.title: L4 Early signs
ladder.slide: Reply time, copies and formal language show a dispute before it explodes. Set a rule with numbers.
ladder.notes: Say: plot the numbers. Check: find trigger week. Mistake: acting only after payment is stopped.

ladder.title: L5 The mediator
ladder.slide: A mediator does not decide. Fairness in place, time and language matters.
ladder.notes: Say: ask who would be trusted. Check: plan fairness. Mistake: choosing a friend of one side.

ladder.title: L6 The mediation order
ladder.slide: Opening, each story, restate, issues, options, agreement. Keep to time.
ladder.notes: Say: use a visible clock. Check: restate step is done. Mistake: skipping the restate.

ladder.title: L7 Plan and governance
ladder.slide: A joint plan has actions, owners, dates, cost split and review rules.
ladder.notes: Say: show a plan that adds up. Check: cost shares sum to total. Mistake: no review date.

rubric.not_yet: Stage or bias is wrong or missing.
rubric.meets: Stage placed correctly and bias named with evidence.
rubric.exceeds: Also estimates the cost of waiting and of acting now.

rubric.not_yet: Steps out of order or one side dominates.
rubric.meets: Steps in order, time kept, both sides heard.
rubric.exceeds: Handles a flare-up calmly and restores the order.

rubric.not_yet: Actions have no owner or the cost split fails to add up.
rubric.meets: Owners, dates and a correct split.
rubric.exceeds: Plan includes a fallback and a trigger for review.

rubric.meets: Triggers, contacts and four numbers with targets.
rubric.exceeds: Targets are realistic, justified from data and short to present.

jobs.what: Handles disagreements between partners, suppliers and teams.
Keeps work moving when two countries disagree on delivery or cost.
Looks after partnerships and runs joint reviews.
Helps staff from different backgrounds settle conflict early.
